s07.slug: SUNDAY · 6:15 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT ROOM — THE FLOOR
body: By the second quarter it is dark on Dupre Street, and the front room is lit by Miami. The green of the field is on every face in the house. Mémère’s lamp makes a yellow island by the window, and through the screen door the porch light is on over the back of Tony’s head. It has not turned around since the coin toss. The Colts are up ten. Twenty-some people are sitting in that ten like a waiting room.

Early in the quarter the Saints get as far as they can get and send out Hartley, and the house watches a forty-six-yard field goal in total silence, the twins’ faces pressed to the rug under the dining table to see it between the chair legs. It goes through. 10–3. Remy kisses the TV screen, and Celeste whispers him off it.

The next time they have the ball they take it the length of the field the slow way, eight yards and six and a first down, Brees throwing short to whoever is open, the room calling out the yard line like bingo. Somewhere around the twenty Lena comes up off the rug onto her knees. Somewhere around the ten she sits back on her heels. Inside the five she sits down again, and back, and her back comes to rest against his shins, where he is sitting against the couch with his knees up. He doesn’t move them.

First and goal. Second. A slip on third down that brings Clovis up out of his chair with both hands on his head. On fourth down at the one nobody comes out to kick, and the whole house understands it together and gets to its feet, Kevin included. Lena doesn’t get up. Her hand comes back over her shoulder without her eyes leaving the screen and finds his wrist where it hangs off his knee, and takes hold, hard, all five fingers. The ball goes into the middle. The middle doesn’t move.

Clovis’s hat is on the floor. Aints III gets up and goes and lies down under the dining table with the twins, who make room. Mémère crosses herself backward, forehead, heart, right shoulder, left, stops, looks at her hand, and does it again correctly with her mouth set. Lena’s fingers come off his wrist one at a time, as if she has only now noticed where they got to, and go back to her lap.
The Colts take it on their own one and run three times into the middle of the field and punt, and the room sits down by degrees and starts, very quietly, to hope again.

Tess gets up from the floor by the television with Lucille on her shoulder, steps over Josie’s feet and around Margot’s footstool, and comes down the room to him. She bends and puts her daughter into his arms over the top of her sister’s head.
“Hold her for me,” she says. “You know how.”

She goes off up the hall toward the kitchen and does not come back. Lucille is asleep in the black-and-gold cap with the fleur-de-lis on top, and she smells of milk and warm wool, and when he gets her into the crook of his left arm her mouth works at a dream and gives up. Lena reaches up without turning around. She finds the baby’s fist by feel, opens it with her thumb, and puts one finger in it, and the fist closes, and Lena puts her head back against his knee and watches the two-minute warning like that.

body.text: Something soft lands on his shoulder from above: a burp cloth, white flannel with ducks on it. “Don’t make it a thing, fireman,” says Laney, from the couch.

body: He turns his head once, to put the Barq’s down on the end of the coffee table out of the baby’s way, and sees the far end of the couch. Laney has a hand on Theo’s knee and the knuckles of it are white. Theo has his eyes on the television and his mouth shut so hard it has gone small and straight. Their eyes go to each other over Jack’s head and over Lena’s, and come away, and Jack catches the tail of it and turns back to the game.

Thirty-some seconds left in the half, and the Saints get the ball back near midfield and move it just far enough. Hartley again, from forty-four, with time for nothing after. It goes through as the clock runs out. 10–6. The room sits down all at once on everything in it that will hold a person, and Clovis picks his hat up off the rug and puts it back on.
On her footstool Margot uncaps a pen and writes in her notebook, steadily, without hurry, and says it as she writes: “Field note. The subjects have stopped pretending the floor is a coincidence.”
“*Margot,*” says Laney.

Lena is already up. She takes her finger back from the baby, and Tess comes down the room for Lucille, and Lena stacks the empty bowls off the rug and the coffee table onto her hip and carries them back through the house to the kitchen, and the back door bangs.

On the television the field is full of people in the dark wheeling a stage on, and then the lights come up all over it, red and white, and two old Englishmen at the middle of it with a band behind them, and the first guitar comes out of the set at a volume Celeste does not allow in this house and allows tonight.
“Who Dat,” Remy says from the arm of the couch, with his cap over his heart. “Who Are You. It’s the same question.”

Over Jack’s head Celeste leans down out of her corner of the couch. She sets a plate of gumbo on the cushion by his ear, rice in the middle, a paper napkin tucked under the rim, and with her foot she slides the empty Igloo across the rug till it touches his knee.
“Baby. Ice. Again,” she whispers. “And Tony hasn’t eaten since the anthem. He won’t come in for it.”

s07t.slug: SUNDAY · 6:55 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH — TONY
body: The cold has come down on the porch while the game was on. It is the first night in New Orleans that feels like February, damp and close, the oak over the street black against the sky, and every porch on Dupre Street is lit. On every one there is a man, or two men, in a chair, with a radio on the rail. The halftime show comes out of the house behind Jack through the screen door, a stadium of drums and a big voice going up, and a few houses down somebody has a window open on the same thing a half second behind.

Tony has his kitchen chair tipped back against the wall under the window and his feet up on the rail beside the radio, a battered silver transistor with a coat hanger for an antenna, turned down so far the WWL halftime men are a murmur of grown men being reasonable. Ferd’s folding chair beside him is empty. Ferd’s cooler isn’t.
Jack holds out the plate.
Tony looks at it, and up at him. “She send you?”
“Yes, sir.”

“Course she did.” He brings his feet down off the rail and the chair down on all four legs and takes the plate on his knees. He eats the first spoonful slowly, like a man reading a contract to the bottom, and nods to himself. He looks up past the porch light at the porch ceiling, painted pale blue.
“Ten–six, Lord,” he says, at no more than his ordinary volume. “I’m not complaining. I’m noting it.” He eats. “We had a deal. I been carrying the account since sixty-seven.”
Jack sits down on the top step with his back against the post.
“Lena tell you about the bag?”
“She did.”

“She tells it wrong.” Tony points the spoon at him. “She tells it like I brought it from home. I paid a dollar for that bag. Man in our section, nineteen-eighty, going up and down the row with a stack of Schwegmann’s bags over his arm like a waiter, a dollar apiece. A *dollar*. Celeste cut the eyeholes in it with her sewing scissors. She had them in her purse. She was twenty years old.” He shakes his head at the street. “Who brings scissors to a football game? I married her for that. One and fifteen, we went. I wore the bag for the last six. This is the forty-third season. Forty-three, son. I been here for forty-one of them.”

Down the block a man on a porch yells something about the second half at the street, and somebody else yells back, *Who dat*, and somebody else answers, and it goes down the street porch to porch and dies out by Esplanade.
Tony eats. With his spoon he points at the floor of the porch, the rail, the steps. “We put this porch back in ’07. My brothers and me. I wanted the steps steep.”

Jack looks down them. From the top step they drop away under the porch light into the dark like a ladder into a ship’s hold, and the sidewalk at the bottom of them is broken up into slabs by the roots of the oak.

body.text: “Your girl in Canada,” Tony says, eating. “She a Colts fan?”
Jack looks at him. Tony goes on eating. “Today,” Jack says.

“Good,” Tony says. “Somebody ought to be.” And that is all of that. He scrapes the edge of the plate for rice and asks Jack, in the same voice, whether Ohio has ever produced a kicker worth a damn, and listens to the answer.

body: The gumbo goes down. Tony is quiet for a stretch, chewing, watching the street, the radio murmuring at his elbow.
“She don’t sleep in cars,” he says.
A spoon of gumbo.
“Two hours to Breaux Bridge on Christmas Eve, two hours back Christmas night, since she was in the car seat. Eyes open. Counting cows.”
He looks at the radio. Jack looks at the radio too. On the WWL halftime the men are going over the fourth down at the one again, and agreeing with each other about it at some length.

choices.text: “Thank you for having us, sir. All six.”
choices.key: At halftime you took Tony a plate on the porch and thanked him for having all six of you. You’re not company, he said.
response: Tony looks at him over the plate.
“You’re not company, son,” he says. “Company don’t get the paddle.”

He scrapes the last of the rice into the spoon and eats it, and hands Jack the plate, empty, with the spoon in it, and Jack takes it. Through the screen door the band brings the last song down on one huge chord that goes on longer than seems possible, and the stadium roars over it, and Tony reaches over with one thick finger and rolls the volume wheel on the transistor until the WWL men are back to their full size. He tips his chair against the wall, puts his feet up on the rail, and shuts his eyes.

choices.text: “In Youngstown we’d have to win one first.”
choices.key: At halftime you took Tony a plate on the porch and told him that in Youngstown they’d have to win one first. He had to put the plate down.
response: It goes into Tony slowly and comes out all at once. He laughs, a huge, helpless, wheezing laugh from the middle of the big body, and the gumbo starts to go over the edge of the plate, and he has to bend down and set it on the boards of the porch beside the chair and put his hands on his knees and laugh into the street. A man two porches down leans out to see what’s funny.
“*Browns*,” Tony tells him, wiping his eyes, and the man nods and goes back in.

Through the screen the halftime show finishes on one long chord and a stadium roaring over the end of it. Tony picks the radio up off the rail and holds it to his ear like a shell, and turns it back up there, and sets it down. The plate stays on the boards by his foot.

choices.text: Ask him what he’ll do if they win.
choices.key: At halftime you took Tony a plate on the porch and asked what he’ll do if they win. Cry on somebody’s car, he said.
response: “If they win,” Jack says. “What will you do?”
Tony doesn’t have to think about it. He has been thinking about it, by the sound of it, most of his life.
“Cry on somebody’s car,” he says.

He goes back to his gumbo. Through the screen the band finishes with one long chord and the stadium in Miami goes up over it, and Tony gives the volume wheel a turn with his thumb and the WWL men come back up out of the murmur, talking fast about the kickoff. He jerks his chin at the door. “Go on in. You’re on the floor.”

s07b.slug: SUNDAY · 6:55 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE SHED — ICE
body: The back steps go down into a yard that has gone cold and blue. The kitchen window is open its crack over the sink, and it throws a yellow square onto the grass and the halftime show out with it, drums and a stadium and a guitar chopping away at the same few chords. The big boil pot is still upside down on the picnic table where it was this afternoon. The burner is a black ring on its stand. At the back of the lot the shed is a white shape under the oak, its door standing open, and out of the door comes a cold white light from low down, and Lena is in the light.

She has pushed the sleeves of her shirt up past the elbows, the way she does, and she is bent over the chest freezer just inside the shed door with both arms in it to the elbow. The freezer’s own bulb comes up on her face from below. Her bowls are stacked in the concrete tub by the shed, rinsed and upside down.
The shed’s light is off. Along the wall, about as high as her shoulder, one board is a little darker than the others in the dark, and he doesn’t look at it long.

He puts the cooler down on the grass at her feet with the lid open. She doesn’t look up. She hands him a bag of ice without a word, and he puts it in, and she hands him another. They are frozen to each other at the corners, and the third one won’t come, so she brings it up out of the freezer two-handed and cracks it down on the freezer’s rim, hard, and the ice inside the plastic goes to gravel, and she hands it to him.
“Mama buys ice like she’s feeding the Easter Vigil,” she says.

Each time she hands a bag across, her fingers are on the plastic where his have to go, and they meet on it, cold on cold, and part, and meet again on the next one. The grass is wet and cold through the canvas of his shoes, and two yards over somebody’s grandmother is out on her own back steps with a cordless phone, telling somebody in Houston about the fourth down in French.

The cold comes up out of the freezer in a slow fog and goes over the rim onto both their hands. It is cold enough out here that what they say shows. The shed door drifts toward him on its hinges in no wind and drifts back, and he puts the side of his shoe against it.

body.text: Lena goes in again, down to the bottom, after the last of it. “You didn’t say it,” she says, into the freezer. “In the car. About her mother.”
He holds the cooler. “It wasn’t mine.”

“I know.” She comes up with a bag of ice against her chest, and frost on the dark hair of her forearms, and puts it in the cooler on top of the others. “That’s the one thing either of us did right in New Mexico.”

Lena straightens with the last bag against her chest and frost on the dark hair of her forearms, and looks at his shoe on the shed door, holding it. “You know about the doors,” she says, and puts the ice in the cooler.

Lena straightens with the last bag against her chest and frost on the dark hair of her forearms, and looks at his shoe on the shed door, holding it. “Daddy hung that door,” she says, and puts the ice in the cooler.

body: Through the kitchen window the band crashes into the next song, and the stadium in Miami sings along.

choices.text: “It was the worst thing I’ve ever said to anybody. The movie.”
choices.key: By the freezer in the shed Lena said you didn’t say it, about Skye’s mother. You told her the movie line was the worst thing you’ve ever said to anybody.
response: He doesn’t take it back. He says what it was.
Lena stands there with her red hands hanging at her sides and looks at him, the freezer light on half her face, for as long as it takes the band to get through a verse.
“I know,” she says. And then, with her chin up: “It was very good, though.”

It almost gets both of them. It gets her: one laugh, short, out of her nose into the cold, with sound to it. It nearly gets him. She shuts the freezer. The light goes off it. They take the cooler up by its two handles, one each, and carry it across the yard and up the back steps, and through the screen door the halftime show is ending on one long chord with a stadium roaring over the top of it.

choices.text: Take the ice out of her hands. Hers are freezing.
choices.key: By the freezer in the shed Lena said you didn’t say it, about Skye’s mother. You took the ice out of her hands and held them till they were warm.
response: Her hands are red to the wrist and stiff, and when she reaches into the freezer again he takes the bag out of them and drops it in the cooler, and takes her hands in his.

They are colder than the ice. He holds them, the two of them together inside his two, and she lets him. Nothing gets said. In the kitchen window the drummer comes in under the guitar, and the song goes on to its end, and the whole time her fingers are getting their feeling back against his palms, he can feel it happen, the stiffness going out of them knuckle by knuckle, until they are only cold, and then only hands.

She takes them back. She shuts the freezer, and the light goes off it, and she bends for her handle of the cooler. They carry it up the back steps together, through the yellow of the kitchen window and into the kitchen light, as the halftime show ends on one long chord with a stadium under it.

choices.key: By the freezer in the shed Lena said you didn’t say it, about Skye’s mother. You said Kevin would want a count. Twelve bags. That’s a prayer.
response: Lena looks down into the cooler. There are five bags in it, one of them in pieces.
“Twelve bags,” she says.
“That’s not a count,” he says. “That’s a prayer.”

“Then he can say it with Mémère.” She shuts the freezer on her side of the argument, and the light goes off, and the yard goes back to the kitchen window. They lift the cooler by its two handles and carry it up the back steps and down the hall, past Mémère’s armchair, where Mémère looks into it as it goes by and says something short in French that makes Lena laugh out loud and not translate. On the television the halftime show is ending on one long chord with a stadium roaring over it.
